newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin replaces top brass, urges military reform.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin replaces top brass, urges military reform.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin stamped his authority on the armed forces and military reforms on Thursday by angrily sacking Defence Minister Igor Rodionov and head of the general staff, Viktor Samsonov.
"They deserved such a decision by doing nothing and they got it," Yeltsin told a meeting of his advisory Defence Council.

Apart from his anger with the apparent failure of the long-awaited military reform, Yeltsin, who announced the sackings at the council meeting, was also clearly furious at the scale of high-level army corruption.
"I am not simply dissatisfied, I am indignant over the state of reforms in the army and the general state of the armed forces," Yeltsin, sounding outraged, told the meeting.
Interfax news agency quoted a statement by Yeltsin's press office as saying he was not satisfied with written proposals on military reform presented by Rodionov and Samsonov.
"Their reports contained no profound principles, military and political, for building the armed forces," the statement said. "They also lacked a financial and economic assessment."
An aide said Yeltsin took the decision to sack Rodionov and Samsonov during the meeting itself, at which he warned that many more heads would roll if the situation did not change.
"The soldier is losing weight while the general is getting fatter," Yeltsin said in reference to high-level corruption scandals embroiling the top brass.

Military prosecutors on Wednesday arrested Konstantin Kobets, one of the country's top generals and a deputy defence minister, previously acclaimed a hero for his defence of Yeltsin in a failed hardline communist coup in 1991.
Kobets is accused of corruption but denies the charges.
Land Forces Commander General Vladimir Semyonov was sacked after corruption charges last month, which he too denies.

Military prosecutors say about 20 generals and 100 colonels are under investigation for graft. Stories abound of army stores, from rations to rockets, being sold off for private profit and of defence contractors building lavish country homes for the top brass in exchange for lucrative army orders.
"We have reached the point when we are short of spoons and plates but the number of servicemen and the number of generals is stubbornly not being cut," Yeltsin said.
Rodionov, 60, was appointed last July under pressure from top brass and Yeltsin's then security adviser Alexander Lebed.
Yeltsin, who is commander-in-chief of the armed forces, promised during his re-election campaign last year to end conscription by 2000 and create a modern, professional army.
But the plan has run into a shortage of funds and a marked lack of enthusiasm in the upper ranks.
"You should be telling me today what you have done. You have nothing to say. Many of you will not be here if you proceed like this," Yeltsin told the meeting.

Rodionov had been at odds with Yeltsin's top defence adviser, Yuri Baturin, over the course of military reforms. The minister said the state must provide more money before change to the underfunded and demoralised force could start.

Baturin, who said Yeltsin had only decided to sack the minister after the Council's meeting had started, has been advocating a different approach. He says reforms should be based on what the state can afford.
Clearly relieved, Baturin later showed television cameras decrees freshly signed by Yeltsin sacking Rodionov and Samsonov.
"Russia cannot afford such expense," Yeltsin said, adding that by 2000 military expenditure should be no more than 3.5 percent of Gross Domestic Product compared to five percent now.
The Kremlin said Yeltsin had appointed 59-year-old Army General Igor Sergeyev, commander of the strategic forces, as acting defence minister.
Baturin told NTV commercial television that Yeltsin also offered Samsonov's job to his loyal ally, Lieutenant General Viktor Chechevatov, commander of the Far East military district.

"Chechevatov asked for time to consider the offer and for a five-minute private conversation with the president," Baturin said. "The conversation took place but the decree (appointing Chechevatov) as far as I know has not been signed."
Yeltsin's press office said it could not confirm an earlier Interfax report about Chechevatov's appointment to the second highest post in the army.

After shaking up the government by promoting a team of young reformers, Yeltsin said he was ready to turn to the military, many of whose 1.8 million men are unhappy after humiliation at the hands of Chechen separatists in the war of 1994-96.
Yeltsin, 66, who was out of action for nearly eight months in 1996 and early this year due to heart problems and then pneumonia, said he would now follow military affairs daily.
